messages.content: Make this more polite for a receptionist to say to a visitor: Tell me your name and number. Then sit there and wait.
May I have your name and number, please? Then please take a seat and wait here.

Sita is meeting an old saintly woman in this Ramayana passage. What would it say in modern prose?

Thus spoke the son of Raghu: she
Approached the saintly devotee,
Who with her white locks, old and frail,
Shook like a plantain in the gale.
To that true spouse she bowed her head,
And "Lady, I am Sita," said:
Raised suppliant hands and prayed her tell
That all was prosperous and well.

After the son of Raghu spoke, Sita went up to the saintly woman, who was old and frail with white hair and trembled like a plantain tree in the wind. Sita bowed her head to that devoted wife and said, "Lady, I am Sita." She raised her hands in respect and asked her to tell her that all was prosperous and well.

Plain prose, please, instead of verse.

Sumantra, at the chief's behest,
Quick to the task himself addressed;
Then near to Rama came, and showed
The chariot ready for the road.
With Sita, then, the princely two,
Who o'er the line of Raghu threw
A glory ever bright and new,
Upon the chariot stood.
Sumantra fast and faster drove
His horses, who in fleetness strove
Still onward to the distant grove,
The hermit-haunted wood.

At Rama's command, Sumantra quickly set about the task himself. Then he came to Rama and showed him the chariot, ready for the road. The two princes, who gave the house of Raghu new and lasting glory, stood on the chariot with Sita. Sumantra drove his horses faster and faster, as they raced each other toward the distant grove, a forest where hermits lived.

Rewrite this in modern English, in four sentences.

Sumantra thus, palm joined to palm,
Poured forth his words of bane and balm,
With keen reproach, with pleading kind,
Striving to move Kaikeyi's mind.
In vain he prayed, in vain reproved,
She heard unsoftened and unmoved.
Nor could the eyes that watched her view
One yielding look, one change of hue.

Sumantra, with his palms joined, spoke words of both warning and comfort, scolding her sharply and pleading kindly, in the hope of changing Kaikeyi's mind. He begged and reproved her in vain. She listened without softening or moving. Those who watched her could see no yielding look and no change in her colour.

Retell this from Arohi's point of view, in the first person.

At the noisy birthday party, Hansa, five, elbowed Arohi, and Arohi's juice spilled on her dress. "Sorry," Hansa said over her shoulder as she grabbed a balloon. Arohi looked at her dress, then at Hansa's back. "She didn't even look at me," she told her mother. Later Hansa came back holding a napkin. "I'm sorry, I'll be careful," she said in a small voice, looking at the stain and then at Arohi's face. Arohi took it and nodded slowly.

At the noisy birthday party, Hansa, five, elbowed me, and my juice spilled on my dress. "Sorry," Hansa said over her shoulder as she grabbed a balloon. I looked at my dress, then at Hansa's back. "She didn't even look at me," I told my mother. Later Hansa came back holding a napkin. "I'm sorry, I'll be careful," she said in a small voice, looking at the stain and then at my face. I took it and nodded slowly.
Make this request polite: Lend me your pen. Mine stopped working.
Could you please lend me your pen? Mine has stopped working.
Change to direct speech: Mother asked me if I had eaten lunch.
Mother asked me, "Have you eaten lunch?"
Loosen this up for a chat: One must endeavour to arrive punctually for the meeting.
Try to get to the meeting on time!
Change the speaker's words into direct speech: Ravi said that he was tired and wanted to go home.
Ravi said, "I am tired and I want to go home."

A brief third-person story, no quotation marks: rewrite this.

"Mashi, look! His face has pictures on it!"
Bidisha glanced at the bus stop. A young man had a tattoo of vines along his jaw. Sachin was staring, mouth open.
"It's called a tattoo, Sachin. Lots of people choose them."
"Does it hurt? Why is it on his face?"
"Good questions. But he can see you staring, and that might feel strange for him."
Sachin looked at his feet. "Am I bad?"
"No, sona. You're curious. Let's wonder quietly and ask me at home."
Sachin nodded and gave the man a small wave.

At the bus stop, Sachin stared, mouth open, at a young man with a tattoo of vines along his jaw, and told his Mashi, Bidisha, that the man's face had pictures on it. Bidisha said it was called a tattoo and that lots of people choose them. Sachin asked whether it hurt and why it was on the man's face. Bidisha said those were good questions, but the man could see him staring, which might feel strange for the man. Sachin looked at his feet and asked whether he was bad. Bidisha said no, he was curious, and suggested they wonder quietly and talk about it at home. Sachin nodded and gave the man a small wave.
Sound more formal when asking: Can you give me change for fifty rupees?
Could you please give me change for fifty rupees?

Rewrite this for a young child, using short sentences and easy words.

Sunaina read the college handbook twice before saying yes to her first paid job. The rule on page fourteen was clear: students may do paid work outside class hours, provided they declare it to the department. She filled the form the same evening.

Sunaina read the college book two times before she said yes to her first job that paid money. The book said students can work after class, but they must tell the college. That evening she filled in the form.

Say this in indirect speech:

Mum told me, "Don't forget to water the tulsi."
Mum told me not to forget to water the tulsi.

Pretend Sana is saying this about herself:

Sana forgot her keys, so she waited outside until her brother came home.
I forgot my keys, so I waited outside until my brother came home.
Use "although" to join these: It was cold. We went swimming.
Although it was cold, we went swimming.
Use the present tense instead: Grandma told us a story and we listened quietly.
Grandma tells us a story and we listen quietly.

Please put this in the present tense.

We sat in the garden. Mum poured the tea and Dad read the newspaper.
We sit in the garden. Mum pours the tea and Dad reads the newspaper.
Polite, please: Come here.
Would you please come here?
Make this formal: I'm really sorry, but I gotta go now.
I am very sorry, but I must leave now.
Use formal English: Tell Mr Rao I called.
Please inform Mr Rao that I called.
